title: Oak cheese board with handle
subtitle: Seasoned wood: a serving board with a long handle, shaped by hand plane and sloyd knife
excerpt: An oak cheese and charcuterie board with a paddle-shaped handle, finished with food-safe board butter. The board is prepared with a hand plane to a flat serving surface, and the handle is shaped with a sloyd knife. Seasoned oak for a board that stays flat and does not absorb moisture during use.
sourceNotes: Cassell's Cyclopaedia of Mechanics vol. III (1885) for the planing and handle-shaping method; Newey & Drage Practical Carpentry for the finishing protocol.

glossaryTerms.definition: A food-safe finish of beeswax and mineral oil. Applied by hand and buffed. Safe for food contact and immediately usable after buffing. The standard finish for cutting boards and kitchen woodware.
Planing or cutting in the direction the wood fibres run, producing a smooth surface. Planing against the grain tears the surface.

content.text: An oak cheese board with a handled paddle shape: a flat 25 cm by 15 cm serving surface and a 12 cm handle that narrows to a rounded grip. Seasoned oak is the right material for a food board, it is dense enough to resist knife marks, and the grain structure means it does not swell and distort in a humid kitchen. The board is finished with
board butter
: food-safe and immediately usable after buffing.
What you need
Wood

One seasoned oak board, 40 cm long (board surface + handle), 15 cm wide, 18, 22 mm thick. The grain must run along the length of the board, a board with cross-grain will warp and eventually crack during kitchen use. English, European, and American white oak are all suitable. Avoid red oak for food-use boards: its open pore structure harbours moisture.
Tools
No. 5 hand plane for flattening and smoothing the serving surface.
Tenon saw for trimming ends and cutting the handle shape.
Sloyd knife for shaping the handle profile.
Sandpaper, 120 and 240 grit.
Leather strop.
Board butter for finishing.
The work
Step 1: Plane the serving face

Secure the board in a vice. Check the face for twist: lay a winding stick across each end and sight along them, any twist shows as the sticks going out of parallel. Remove twist with diagonal plane passes. Then plane the whole face
with the grain
until it is flat and smooth. Oak planes well with a sharp No. 5; if the surface tears, check the grain direction and reverse.
Step 2: Mark and cut the handle outline

On the back of the board, draw the handle profile: 12 cm from one end, the board narrows from 15 cm width to 4 cm at the grip. Mark the taper with a pencil. Use the tenon saw to cut the two straight cuts that remove the waste at each side of the handle, then clean up the curve at the shoulder with the sloyd knife using
push cuts
Step 3: Shape and round the handle

Use the sloyd knife to chamfer the edges of the handle on all four corners, removing the sharp arris and producing a comfortable rounded grip. The serving face edge of the board is given a gentle chamfer to remove the sharp corner. Sand all surfaces progressively: 120 grit to remove plane marks, 240 grit to finish. Always sand with the grain.
Finishing

Apply board butter by hand to all surfaces, working it into the grain. Leave for 10 minutes, then buff off the excess with a clean cloth. The board is immediately food-safe. Re-apply every three to six months or when the wood starts to look dry.
Variations
Walnut board: darker colour and finer grain. Use the same method.
Serving board without handle: square ends, 35 cm by 20 cm.

attrs.symptom: The plane tears the surface in streaks rather than producing a smooth finish
attrs.cause: Planing against the grain or interlocked grain in the oak is tearing fibres
attrs.fix: Check grain direction by watching the shavings, if they come off in broken pieces and the surface is rough, reverse the planing direction. For interlocked grain (visible as a ribbon figure on the surface), plane diagonally at 45 degrees to the grain, then finish with light passes along the grain.
